Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) publishes a record of every work-related
death since 1991: what happened, in which industry, at what size of workplace, and what kind of
accident it was. This notebook uses 1991 to 2024. Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/jp-mhlw-fatal-accidents/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           guess_max = 60000,
           # Codes such as "01" are text, not numbers
           col_types = cols(industry_sector_code = "c", industry_group_code = "c",
                            industry_detail_code = "c", agent_group_code = "c",
                            agent_subgroup_code = "c", agent_detail_code = "c",
                            accident_type_code = "c"))
}

deaths <- read_module("tidy", "fatalities.csv.gz")
nrow(deaths)
```

Each row is one person killed. The descriptions (`narrative_ja`) are in Japanese; for 2024 there is
also an English translation (`narrative_en`).

# Part 1. Fewer deaths

```{r trend}
by_year <- count(deaths, year, name = "deaths")

ggplot(by_year, aes(year, deaths)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths in Japan", x = NULL, y = "Deaths")

by_year |> filter(year %in% c(1991, 2000, 2010, 2024))
```

**Questions**

1. By how much did deaths fall from 1991 to 2024 (as a number and a percentage)?
2. Japan's employed workforce was roughly the same size in 2024 as in 1991. What does that tell
   you about the death *rate*?

   number that has not fallen since the early 2000s. Japan has about 40% of the US population.
   Before concluding Japan's workplaces are safer, what differences in *coverage* would you check?
   (See the README's limitations.)

# Part 2. Which industries?

```{r industries}
deaths |>
  filter(year %in% c(1991, 2024)) |>
  count(year, industry_sector) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3)) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = share, names_prefix = "share_") |>
  arrange(desc(share_2024))

deaths |>
  mutate(sector = fct_lump_n(industry_sector, 5)) |>
  count(year, sector) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, n, fill = sector)) +
  geom_area() +
  labs(title = "Deaths by industry sector", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which sector has the most deaths? What share of deaths was in construction in 1991 and in 2024?
2. Which sectors have fallen fastest, and which have changed least?
3. Many deaths in "Transport" are truck drivers. Would you count a truck driver killed in a road
   crash as an occupational death? How does the CFOI treat them?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. How do workers die?

```{r how}
deaths |>
  filter(year >= 2020) |>
  count(accident_type, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3)) |>
  head(10)

# Falls from height: what did people fall from?
deaths |>
  filter(year >= 2020, accident_type == "Fall from height") |>
  count(agent_subgroup, agent_detail_ja, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)

deaths |>
  filter(accident_type %in% c("Fall from height", "Traffic accident (road)",
                              "Caught in or between", "Struck by moving object")) |>
  count(year, accident_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, n, colour = accident_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Deaths by type of accident", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", colour = NULL)
```

The detailed agents are in Japanese. Common ones: 「足場」 scaffold, 「屋根、はり、もや、けた、
合掌」 roofs and roof beams, 「はしご等」 ladders, 「開口部」 openings, 「階段、桟橋」 stairs
and gangways, 「トラック」 trucks, 「建築物、構築物」 buildings and structures.

**Questions**

1. What are the three most common types of fatal accident since 2020?
2. Which type of accident has fallen most since 1991? Suggest a reason.
3. What do workers most often fall from? For the top two, name a control at each level of the
   hierarchy of controls (elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE).

# Part 4. When?

```{r when}
deaths |>
  count(month) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(month), n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Deaths by month, 1991 to 2024", x = "Month", y = "Deaths")

# Heat: contact with hot objects includes heatstroke
deaths |>
  filter(accident_type_code == "11") |>
  count(month)

# Time of day (1-hour bands, 1991 to 2018)
deaths |>
  filter(year <= 2018, !is.na(hour_start)) |>
  count(hour_start) |>
  ggplot(aes(hour_start, n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Deaths by hour of day, 1991 to 2018", x = "Hour starting", y = "Deaths")
```

**Questions**

1. Are some months more dangerous than others? Which accident type peaks in July and August?
2. Describe the pattern by hour of day. Why is there a dip at noon? Why might deaths at 8 to 11 am
   and 2 to 5 pm be most common?
3. From 2019 MHLW records the time in 2-hour bands. Why does that matter if you want to combine
   years?

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Reading the descriptions

The English translations of the 2024 descriptions were made with an AI model for this course and
are not official; the Japanese is authoritative.

```{r narratives}
d2024 <- filter(deaths, year == 2024, !is.na(narrative_en))
nrow(d2024)

# Search the English descriptions (change the search term)
forklift <- filter(d2024, str_detect(str_to_lower(narrative_en), "forklift"))
nrow(forklift)
set.seed(1)
forklift |>
  slice_sample(n = 3) |>
  pull(narrative_en)

# Japanese search works on every year: 熱中症 means heatstroke
heat <- "熱中症"
deaths |>
  filter(str_detect(narrative_ja, heat)) |>
  count(year) |>
  filter(year >= 2015)
```

**Questions**

1. Read three of the forklift deaths. For each, name the hazard and one control that would have
   prevented the death.
2. Search the 2024 descriptions for another hazard (for example "ladder", "roof", "tree" or
   "heatstroke"). What do the deaths have in common?
3. MHLW's separate heatstroke statistics count about 30 heatstroke deaths a year recently. How many
   does the search for 熱中症 find? Why might a search of short descriptions miss some?
